> 其政悶悶，其民淳淳；其政察察，其民缺缺.

Chapter 57 gave a prescription: don't add affairs. Chapter 58 explains why the prescription has to be taken.

Two pairs of eyes, and one shut and one turning things over.

## 悶 is a heart shut behind a door

悶: 懑也, built on 心 and 門. The heart is inside the door.

So 其政悶悶 is not "the government is muddled." It is: the affairs are kept behind the door — not brought out, not circulated.

## 察 is to cover and turn over

察: 覆也, built on 宀 (the roof) and 祭 (the offering). To cover something under a roof and examine it.

So 其政察察 is not "the government is clear-sighted." It is: everything is brought under the roof and turned over and inspected.

## 淳淳 and 缺缺

淳: the unadulterated, the thick and simple. 缺: the vessel with a broken rim.

The pairing is exact and it is an exchange rate: the closed door produces the whole people; the turning-over produces a chipped people.

Not because inspection is cruel, but because inspection is a process that requires each thing to have a flaw to find. A system that looks for flaws converts a population into a set of defect sites.

## 禍兮，福之所倚；福兮，禍之所伏

Calamity — that is where good fortune leans. Good fortune — that is where calamity is hidden.

倚 is to lean against; 伏 is to lie concealed. Both are positional words, and neither says which comes first. They describe two things in the same place.

## 孰知其極？其無正也

Who knows its limit? There is no 正.

Return to chapter 57's 正: a foot stopping where it should. 其無正 also: there is no position where the foot can settle, because the ground is moving under it.

That is not moral relativism; it is a description of the limits of prediction.

## 正復為奇，善復為妖

The aligned becomes the unpaired; the good becomes the 妖.

妖 is not "demon." It is the abnormal, the thing that has grown into an unusual form — the same family as 夭, the premature.

So the sentence says: what is standard turns odd, and what is praised turns strange. The reversal is not a moral failure; it is what time does to any fixed standard.

## 人之迷，其日固久

People's confusion has been solid for a long time. 固 — firmly, not recently.

The line is generous: this is not a new mistake.

## The four 而's

> 是以聖人方而不割，廉而不劌，直而不肆，光而不耀.

方: 併船也 — two boats lashed together. So 方而不割 is "joined, and not cut apart." Not "square and not cutting": the image is two hulls bound side by side.

廉: the edge of a thing, the corner. 劌: to cut, to wound. 廉而不劌 — has an edge and does not wound with it.

直而不肆 — straight and not unrestrained. 肆 is to extend to the limit.

光而不耀 — has light and does not glare. 耀 is the flash that makes others squint.

All four are the same shape: the quality is present, and its aggressive form is withheld. Each is a thing that is real and does not announce its edge.

## The chapter's place

Chapter 57: the ruler adds nothing.
Chapter 58: the reason is that the ground moves, so a fixed standard cannot hold.

And the four 而's are what a person looks like who knows this and still acts: joined but not cutting, edged but not wounding.

## A test

Take the standard you are most confident about. Then ask: what would it look like in ten years if the ground moved? If you can't imagine it turning strange, that is 迷, and it has been solid for a while.
